exam: 1. A 65‑year‑old post‑surgery patient develops watery diarrhoea 48h after broad‑spectrum antibiotics. What is the next step? — Order stool toxin ELISA/PCR; start oral vancomycin if positive; consider stool culture if resources allow.
2. A patient with C. diff presents with abdominal distension and tachycardia. What is the most likely complication? — Toxic megacolon; urgent surgical consultation and bowel rest are required.

3. Why is fidaxomicin preferred over metronidazole in severe C. diff? — Fidaxomicin has lower recurrence rates and is bactericidal against C. diff spores, whereas metronidazole is less effective and has higher toxicity.

4. A patient on vancomycin develops persistent diarrhoea after 7 days. What should you do? — Switch to fidaxomicin or consider a prolonged vancomycin course; evaluate for recurrence with repeat toxin test.
5. Which infection control measure is most effective against C. diff in a low‑resource setting? — Hand washing with soap and water; alcohol rubs are inadequate against spores.

6. How does C. diff toxin lead to pseudomembrane formation? — Toxins activate Rho GTPases, causing cytoskeletal disruption, cell death, and accumulation of neutrophils and necrotic debris forming pseudomembranes.
ai.title: Clostridioides difficile Infection
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: A toxin‑producing anaerobe that causes antibiotic‑associated diarrhoea and pseudomembranous colitis, common in hospitals and increasingly in the community, especially after broad‑spectrum antibiotics.

sections.p: Clostridioides difficile is a gram‑positive, spore‑forming anaerobe that thrives when normal gut flora are disrupted, most often by antibiotics.

b: Toxin A: enterotoxin; Toxin B: cytotoxin; both bind to cell receptors and activate Rho GTPases
sections.p: The organism produces two exotoxins, TcdA and TcdB, which damage colonic epithelium and trigger inflammation.

b: Fomite transmission; hand hygiene essential; spores resistant to alcohol
sections.p: Spores are hardy, survive on surfaces for months, and are spread via hand contact or contaminated equipment.

b: Mild: watery diarrhoea, abdominal cramp; Severe: fever, leukocytosis, abdominal distension, toxic megacolon
sections.p: Antibiotic‑associated diarrhoea progressing to pseudomembranous colitis; severity ranges from mild watery stools to toxic megacolon.

b: Clinical criteria: ≥3 unformed stools in 24h after antibiotics
sections.p: Clinical suspicion plus laboratory confirmation of toxin or PCR; microscopy of stool for pseudomembranes is rarely used.

t.b: Detects TcdA/TcdB; positive means active toxin production
Highly sensitive; positive confirms infection even if toxin not detected
Identifies organism but not toxin status; used if resources allow

sections.p: First‑line therapy is oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin; metronidazole is reserved for mild disease or when first‑line drugs are unavailable.

t.b: Prevents spread; alcohol ineffective against spores

b: Toxin ELISA positive = active disease; negative but high suspicion → PCR
sections.p: Remember that C. diff is a toxin‑mediated disease; diagnosis relies on stool toxin or PCR, not just culture. In severe cases, look for toxic megacolon signs and consider surgery.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with distension, fever >38.5°C, leukocytosis >15,000/µL, or signs of toxic megacolon (rigid abdomen, tachycardia, hypotension)
